title: Work in Progress Is Not Revenue: The Number Most Engineering and Architecture Firms Never Watch
excerpt: World Town Planning Day is a reminder of how project-based engineering and architecture work really is. The bigger risk rarely shows up in the pipeline. It shows up in unbilled work in progress.
content:
World Town Planning Day falls today, a modest nod to the planners, engineers and architects who shape how Australian cities and regions grow. For the firms behind that work, the sharper commercial story rarely has anything to do with planning approvals. It has to do with a number sitting quietly in the accounts that almost never gets the same attention as the pipeline.

That number is work in progress, or WIP. It is the value of design and engineering work a firm has already completed but has not yet invoiced, and in a lot of Queensland and Sydney practices, it has been left to grow for months, treated as an accounting entry rather than a cash flow problem.

A firm can look genuinely profitable on its profit and loss statement and still be short on cash, because the P&L recognises work as it is delivered, not as it is paid for. WIP is the gap between those two realities, and it widens every week a project sits between a completed design stage and an invoice that has not yet gone out the door.

Why WIP Builds Up on Multi-Stage Projects

Engineering and architecture work rarely bills in one clean hit. A typical project moves through concept design, development application support, detailed documentation and construction phase services, often across many months. Each stage usually carries a notional billing milestone, but the trigger for raising that invoice is rarely automatic. It depends on a director reviewing the deliverable, a client signing off a stage, or a practice simply waiting for a natural pause in the workload to catch up on invoicing.

Scope variations compound the pattern. A client asks for a design change midway through documentation, the team absorbs the extra hours to keep the project moving, and the variation gets logged for billing later rather than invoiced as it happens. Later rarely arrives on schedule. By the time a firm reconciles its WIP at year end, it is common to find a sizeable amount of completed, chargeable work that was never formally claimed.

The WIP Figure That Deserves the Same Attention as the Pipeline

Most practices track their forward pipeline closely, because a thin pipeline feels like an obvious risk. WIP rarely gets the same scrutiny, because a growing WIP balance looks like a sign of a busy, successful firm rather than cash that has already been earned and is simply sitting unclaimed. The two numbers deserve equal billing in a monthly review, since one measures the work ahead and the other measures the cash already owed to the business for work behind it.

An ageing report run against WIP, grouped by project and by the stage each job has reached, usually surfaces the pattern quickly. A handful of long-running projects, often the larger and more complex ones with the most senior staff attached, tend to carry the bulk of the unbilled balance. These are rarely disputes. They are simply jobs where the invoicing step has fallen behind the delivery step, and nobody owns closing that gap on a fixed cadence.

Turning WIP Into a Weekly Cash Number

The firms that manage this well treat invoicing as a stage of project delivery, not an administrative task that happens whenever someone finds the time. Billing milestones get tied to a specific, observable trigger, such as a stage sign-off or a certified progress claim, rather than to a vague sense that enough time has passed. Variations get logged and billed within the same invoicing cycle as the work that triggered them, rather than banked for a conversation at project close.

A Working Capital Unlock project typically starts exactly here, mapping WIP alongside debtors and supplier terms to show where cash is genuinely trapped rather than simply delayed, then building a billing cadence that keeps pace with delivery instead of running months behind it. For many Queensland and New South Wales consultancies, closing that gap releases cash the firm had already earned months earlier, without a single additional hour of billable work.

A full pipeline and a growing WIP balance can look identical from the outside, both signs of a busy, in-demand practice. The difference only shows up in the bank account, and by then the gap has usually been funded out of whatever buffer the firm happened to be carrying. Many engineering and architecture firms bring in a fractional CFO specifically to own this number on an ongoing basis, reviewing WIP alongside the pipeline every month rather than discovering the gap at year end. faqs.q: What does work in progress mean for an engineering or architecture firm?
faqs.a: Work in progress, or WIP, is the value of design, engineering or documentation work a firm has already completed but has not yet invoiced to the client. It sits in the accounts as an asset, but unlike cash in the bank, it cannot cover payroll or supplier bills until it is actually billed and collected, which is why a growing WIP balance deserves the same scrutiny as the pipeline of future work.

faqs.q: Why can a busy engineering or architecture firm still run short on cash?
faqs.a: A firm's profit and loss statement recognises work as it is delivered, not as it is paid for, so a practice can look genuinely profitable while a large amount of completed work sits unbilled as WIP. The busier the firm, the more work typically sits in that gap at any given time, which is why strong activity and tight cash can show up in the same month.

faqs.q: How often should a consultancy review its WIP ageing report?
faqs.a: A monthly review is the useful rhythm for most engineering and architecture practices, run alongside the pipeline review rather than separately from it. Grouping WIP by project and by the stage each job has reached usually shows quickly which jobs have fallen behind on invoicing. Building this into regular cash flow discipline keeps the gap from quietly growing between reviews.

faqs.q: What is the difference between WIP and debtors on a firm's balance sheet?
faqs.a: WIP is work that has been completed but not yet invoiced, while debtors are invoices that have been issued but not yet paid. Both represent cash tied up outside the bank account, but they sit at different points in the cycle and usually need different fixes, invoicing discipline for WIP and collections discipline for debtors, so it helps to track them as two separate numbers rather than one combined figure.

faqs.q: How does a fractional CFO help an engineering or architecture firm manage WIP?
faqs.a: A fractional CFO typically takes ownership of the monthly WIP and pipeline review, setting clear billing milestones tied to project stages and following up on variations before they age into a year-end surprise. For firms with several concurrent multi-stage projects, having one person accountable for this number tends to matter more than any single process change.

faqs.q: What does a Working Capital Unlock project involve for a professional services firm?
faqs.a: A Working Capital Unlock maps where cash is genuinely trapped across WIP, debtors and supplier terms, then produces a prioritised action list to release it. For engineering and architecture practices, the WIP side of that review is often where the largest and least expected amount of already-earned cash is found sitting unclaimed.
